This is probably to be expected, the call when returning to an await isn't the same call context as it's resumed, might be possible to save it but it's technically not incorrect to have that be lost

Functionally things work like this:
```gdscript
func func_1():
    func_2()
    await signal_x
    func_3()
```
Is equivalent to
```gdscript
func func_1():
    func_2()
    signal_x.connect(func_1_rest, CONNECT_ONE_SHOT)

func func_1_rest():
    func_3()
```
I see, though I would like to know where a function was called from for debugging

Absolutely, it might not be trivial to do though, and we'd have to make it work for this exception somehow, because I don't think you'd expect this behavior in other cases, for example an error in a callback for a signal connected from `_ready` (probably not a real risk as it uses its own internal system but might be a limitation to save the stack data)

This isn't a bug, but a missing feature (I'd recommend opening a proposal instead). When a coroutine pauses, control in the current thread is returned to the calling function, so the call stack may change when the coroutine resumes. Implementing this feature can be challenging and requires considering various details. At a minimum, the following things come to mind: 1. Saved frames should be displayed in a different color in the debugger to reduce confusion. Or perhaps they should be displayed as a separate "Corouine Context" item, expanding into a subtree. 2. The saved call stack shouldn't store local variables (at least objects, arrays, and dictionaries), as this can have side effects on memory management. 3. It's important to consider that the current call stack may contain multiple chains of regular methods and continued coroutines, intermingled. 4. A coroutine can be continued in a different thread than the one in which it was created. Displaying the old call stack in a new thread would be confusing without proper indication. Also, it's a bit difficult to visualize the "combining" of threads (the context in which the coroutine was created plus the context in which it is continued). This is especially true if the call stack contains multiple coroutine continuations and/or the coroutine has been suspended and continued multiple times. This will no longer be a flat list, but a tree or perhaps even a graph. 5. Infinite recursions. Currently, you can recursively call a function after a proper `await`, and it won't cause either a stack overflow or extra memory consumption. If we keep the call stack for coroutine continuations, this will lead to the second (but not the first, since this information will have to be stored on the heap anyway, not on the stack). This is another reason why we should consider whether it's worth storing local variables (even of value types). Also, note that the call stack doesn't always reflect the "true" call sequence. Rather, it's the context of the current thread's pending calls. When a function starts, a frame is added to the call stack; when it finishes, the frame is removed. Just because two frames are adjacent in the call stack doesn't mean one function calls another. For example, a GDScript function can be called by the core or another scripting language.
